Provides a centralized schema definition management solution, standardizing and simplifying schema handling.

## Motivation

- Unifies fragmented schema implementations into a single maintainable module.
- Ensures schema adherence to JSON Schema Draft-7+.

## High-Level Principles

- Clear and informative schema validation.
- Strong typing with explicit typespecs.
- Comprehensive documentation and ease of reuse.

## Core Relationships

```
                       +--------------------------+
                       | Alaigned.Schema.Definition|
                       +-------------+------------+
                                     |
                                     v
                       +--------------------------+
                       | Alaigned.Schema.Parser   |
                       +-------------+------------+
                                     |
                                     v
                       +--------------------------+
                       | Alaigned.Schema.Validator|
                       +-------------+------------+
                                     |
             +-----------+-----------+-----------+
             |           |                       |
             v           v                       v
  +-----------------+  +----------------+  +----------------+
  |    Generator    |  |    Serializer  |  |   Normalizer   |
  +-----------------+  +----------------+  +----------------+
```

## Alaigned.Seeder – Macro-Based Interface for Entity Seeders

This module provides a `use` macro for implementing declarative, standardized
data seeders in the Alaigned system. It injects default implementations for:

  * `seed/1`
  * `reset/1`
  * `status/0`
  * `upsert/1`
  * `load_records/1`

Each seeder can specify:

  * `@schema` – target Ecto schema
  * `@priority` – order of execution
  * `@fixture_path` – optional path to JSON data
  * `@default_data` – optional hardcoded data fallback
  * `@upsert_keys` – conflict resolution fields

## Example

    defmodule Alaigned.Seeder.Entities.UsersSeeder do
      use Alaigned.Seeder,
        name: :users,
        priority: 10,
        schema: Alaigned.Accounts.User,
        upsert_keys: [:email],
        default_data: [%{"email" => "admin@alaigned.com", "username" => "admin"}]
    end

## Behavior

Implements `Alaigned.Seeder.Behaviour`.

## Doctests

    iex> Module.concat(Alaigned.Seeder.Entities.UsersSeeder).name()
    :users

    iex> Module.concat(Alaigned.Seeder.Entities.UsersSeeder).priority()
    10

    iex> Module.concat(Alaigned.Seeder.Entities.UsersSeeder).status() in [
    ...>   :not_seeded,
    ...>   {:seeded, _}
    ...> ]
    true

Sends a prompt to ChatGPT and returns the response.

Submits the given prompt to the ChatGPT API along with any conversation history
that has been accumulated in the client. Returns both the response text and an
updated client with the new message history.

## Parameters

* `client` - A ChatGPT client struct
* `prompt` - The text prompt to send to ChatGPT
* `opts` - Optional keyword list of parameters to override for this request:
  * `:temperature` - Override the temperature setting
  * `:max_tokens` - Override the max_tokens setting

## Returns

* `{:ok, updated_client, response}` - Successfully received a response
* `{:error, client, error_message}` - Failed to get a response

## Examples

    iex> client = ChatGPT.new(%{api_key: "sk-test"})
    ...> {:ok, updated_client, response} = ChatGPT.ask(client, "Hello, how are you?")
    ...> is_binary(response)
    true
    iex> length(updated_client.messages)
    2

    # With custom parameters for this request only
    iex> client = ChatGPT.new(%{api_key: "sk-test"})
    ...> 
    ...> {:ok, updated_client, response} =
    ...>   ChatGPT.ask(client, "Write a creative story", temperature: 0.9, max_tokens: 2000)

Configuration struct for ChatGPT client with specific parameters.

This struct holds all configuration options for the ChatGPT client,

* `:finch_name` - Custom Finch pool name
* `:headers` - Additional HTTP headers
* `:options` - Additional model parameters

module_attributes.value:
OpenAI ChatGPT API client implementation using the OpenaiEx library.

This module provides an implementation of the `Prismatic.LLM.Client` behaviour
for interacting with OpenAI's ChatGPT models. It handles configuration,
message history tracking, and communication with the OpenAI API.

## Features

* Full support for ChatGPT models (gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, etc.)
* Conversation context management
* Configurable API parameters (temperature, max_tokens, etc.)
* Custom API endpoints support
* Timeout configuration

## Basic Usage

```elixir
# Create a new client with the OpenAI API key
client = Prismatic.LLM.Clients.ChatGPT.new(%{api_key: System.get_env("OPENAI_API_KEY")})

# Send a message to ChatGPT
{:ok, client, response} = Prismatic.LLM.Clients.ChatGPT.ask(client, "Hello, how can you help me?")

# The client keeps track of the conversation history
# Send a follow-up question
{:ok, client, response} = Prismatic.LLM.Clients.ChatGPT.ask(client, "Tell me more about that.")
```

## Configuration

The client can be configured with various options:

```elixir
client = Prismatic.LLM.Clients.ChatGPT.new(%{
  api_key: System.get_env("OPENAI_API_KEY"),
  model: "gpt-4o",
  temperature: 0.5,
  max_tokens: 2000,
  # organization: "your-organization-id", # Optional
  # base_url: "http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1", # Optional
  receive_timeout: 30_000 # Optional
})
```

## Advanced Usage

You can update the client configuration at any time:

```elixir
# Update temperature for a specific request
updated_client = Prismatic.LLM.Clients.ChatGPT.update_config(client, %{temperature: 0.9})

# Or provide options directly in the ask method
{:ok, client, response} = Prismatic.LLM.Clients.ChatGPT.ask(
  client,
  "Generate a creative story",
  [temperature: 0.9, max_tokens: 2000]
)
```

Merges two maps deeply, keeping nested structures intact.

This function performs a recursive merge of two maps, ensuring that nested maps
are properly merged rather than being overwritten.

## Parameters
  - `left` - The base map
  - `right` - The map to merge on top of the base map

## Returns
  - A new map with the merged contents of both input maps

## Examples

    iex> left = %{a: 1, b: %{c: 2, d: 3}}
    ...> right = %{b: %{c: 10, e: 4}, f: 5}
    ...> Prismatic.LLM.Client.deep_merge(left, right)
    %{a: 1, b: %{c: 10, d: 3, e: 4}, f: 5}

    iex> Prismatic.LLM.Client.deep_merge(%{a: 1}, %{a: 2})
    %{a: 2}

    iex> Prismatic.LLM.Client.deep_merge(%{a: %{b: 1}}, %{a: %{c: 2}})
    %{a: %{b: 1, c: 2}}

Extracts the last assistant message from a conversation history.

This function scans through a list of messages (in reverse order) to find
the most recent message from the assistant role.

## Parameters
  - `messages` - A list of message maps with `role` and `content` keys

## Returns
  - The content of the last assistant message, or `nil` if no assistant message is found

## Examples

    iex> messages = [
    ...>   %{role: "user", content: "Hello"},
    ...>   %{role: "assistant", content: "Hi, how can I help?"},
    ...>   %{role: "user", content: "Tell me about Elixir."},
    ...>   %{role: "assistant", content: "Elixir is a functional programming language."}
    ...> ]
    ...> 
    ...> Prismatic.LLM.Client.last_response(messages)
    "Elixir is a functional programming language."

    iex> Prismatic.LLM.Client.last_response([])
    nil

    iex> Prismatic.LLM.Client.last_response([%{role: "user", content: "Hello"}])
    nil

Sends a query to the LLM and returns an updated client struct with the response.

This callback should be implemented by each client to handle the specifics of
communicating with their respective LLM service.

  - `client` - The client struct
  - `prompt` - The text prompt to send to the LLM
  - `opts` - Additional options for this specific request

## Returns
  - `{:ok, updated_client, response}` on success
  - `{:error, client, error_message}` on failure

## Example Implementation

    @impl true
    def ask(client, prompt, opts \ []) do
      client = add_message(client, prompt)

      case MyAPI.Client.complete(client.api_client, client.messages, opts) do
        {:ok, response} ->
          updated_client = add_message(client, response, "assistant")
          {:ok, updated_client, response}

        {:error, reason} ->
          {:error, client, "API request failed: #{inspect(reason)}"}
      end
    end

Sends a message to the llama.cpp server and returns the response.

This function takes the current client state, adds the user's message to the
conversation history, sends the entire conversation to the llama.cpp server,
and returns the updated client with the response.

## Parameters

* `client` - The Llama client
* `prompt` - The user's message
* `opts` - Additional options that override the client's configuration

## Options

* `:temperature` - Override the default temperature
* `:max_tokens` - Override the default max tokens
* `:stream` - Whether to stream the response
* `:stream_callback` - Function to call with each chunk when streaming

## Examples

```elixir
# Simple request
{:ok, updated_client, response} = Prismatic.LLM.Clients.Llama.ask(client, "Hello!")

# With overridden options
{:ok, updated_client, response} = Prismatic.LLM.Clients.Llama.ask(
  client,
  "Generate a creative story",
  temperature: 0.9,
  max_tokens: 2000
)

# With streaming
{:ok, updated_client, response} = Prismatic.LLM.Clients.Llama.ask(
  client,
  "Tell me a long story",
  stream: true,
  stream_callback: fn chunk -> IO.write(chunk) end
)
```

Creates a new Llama client with the given configuration.

## Parameters

* `config` - Configuration struct or map/keyword list with configuration values

## Configuration Options

* `:base_url` - URL of the llama.cpp server (required)
* `:model` - Name of the model (optional, for logging)
* `:temperature` - Controls randomness (default: 0.7)
* `:max_tokens` - Maximum tokens to generate (default: 1024)
* `:stop` - List of sequences that will cause the model to stop generating
* `:repeat_penalty` - Penalty for repeated tokens (default: 1.1)
* `:top_k` - Limit to top K tokens (default: 40)
* `:top_p` - Nucleus sampling threshold (default: 0.95)
* `:timeout` - Request timeout in milliseconds (default: 60000)
* `:stream` - Whether to stream the response (default: false)
* `:options` - Additional options to pass to the API

## Examples

```elixir
# Create with struct
config = Prismatic.LLM.Clients.Llama.Config.new(
  base_url: "http://localhost:8080",
  model: "llama-3-8b",
  temperature: 0.8
)
client = Prismatic.LLM.Clients.Llama.new(config)

# Create with map
client = Prismatic.LLM.Clients.Llama.new(%{
  base_url: "http://localhost:8080",
  temperature: 0.8
})

# Create with keyword list
client = Prismatic.LLM.Clients.Llama.new(
  base_url: "http://localhost:8080",
  max_tokens: 2000
)
```

Client implementation for llama.cpp through its HTTP server interface.

This client allows interaction with the llama.cpp server, which provides
a REST API for interacting with local LLM models.

## Setup

1. Make sure you have llama.cpp installed and the server running:
   ```bash
   ./server --model models/llama-3-8b.Q4_0.gguf --chat-template chatml
   ```

2. Create a Llama client:
   ```elixir
   llama = Prismatic.LLM.Clients.Llama.new(%{
     base_url: "http://localhost:8080",
     model: "llama-3-8b"
   })
   ```

3. Interact with the model:
   ```elixir
   {:ok, llama, response} = Prismatic.LLM.Clients.Llama.ask(llama, "Hello, how are you?")
   ```

When used, defines a struct based on the JSON schema located at the specified path.

* `:root_namespace` - Base namespace for referenced schemas (optional)

## Examples

```elixir
# Basic usage

end

# Using from a specific definition in the schema
defmodule MyApp.Admin do

    schema_path: "priv/schemas/user.json",
    definition: "AdminUser"
end

# Using with a root namespace for nested references
defmodule MyApp.Product do
  use Core.JsonSchemaStruct,
    schema_path: "priv/schemas/product.json",
    root_namespace: MyApp
end
```

## Generated Functions

The following functions are generated for the module:

* `validate/1` - Validates a struct against the schema constraints
* Type specifications for all fields

## Generated Struct

A struct is defined with fields from the schema properties, using appropriate
default values based on the schema types.

module_attributes.name: moduledoc
module_attributes.value:
Generates Elixir structs from JSON Schema definitions at compile time.

This module provides macros that read JSON schema files during compilation,
parse their structure, and generate corresponding Elixir modules with structs,
typespecs, and validation functions.

## Features

* Creates Elixir structs with appropriate default values based on JSON schema types
* Generates type specifications for all fields
* Provides validation based on schema constraints (required, minLength, maxLength, etc.)
* Supports nested structures and field references
* Compatible with Ecto and other struct-based libraries

## Installation

Add to your dependencies:

```elixir
defp deps do
  [
    {:core_json_schema_struct, "~> 0.1.0"}
  ]
end
```

## Basic Usage

Define a schema file (e.g., `priv/schemas/user.json`):

```json
{
  "title": "User",
  "description": "A user account",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "username": {
      "type": "string",
      "minLength": 3,
      "maxLength": 20
    },
    "email": {
      "type": "string",
      "format": "email"
    },
    "age": {
      "type": "integer",
      "minimum": 18
    },
    "active": {
      "type": "boolean",
      "default": true
    }
  },
  "required": ["username", "email"]
}
```

Then, in your module:

```elixir
defmodule MyApp.User do
  use Core.JsonSchemaStruct, schema_path: "priv/schemas/user.json"
end
```

Now you can create and validate structs:

```elixir
# Create a user (with defaults applied)
user = %MyApp.User{username: "john_doe", email: "john@example.com", age: 25}

# Validate according to schema constraints
case MyApp.User.validate(user) do
  {:ok, valid_user} -> # use valid_user
  {:error, %{errors: errors}} -> # handle validation errors
end
```

Creates a stream from an Ecto query.

## Options

  * `:batch_size` - The number of records to fetch per batch (default: `100`)
  * `:strategy` - The pagination strategy to use: `:offset` or `:keyset` (default: `:offset`)
  * `:cursor_fields` - Fields to use for keyset pagination (default: `[:id]`).
    Should be indexed fields, and match the `order_by` clause for optimal performance.
  * `:transform` - Function to transform each result (default: `Function.identity/1`)
  * `:timeout` - Timeout for each database query (default: `15_000` ms)
  * `:telemetry` - Enable telemetry events (default: `true`)
  * `:max_retries` - Maximum number of retry attempts for transient errors (default: `3`)

## Example

    query = from(p in Post, order_by: [desc: p.inserted_at, asc: p.id])
    stream = QueryStream.new(query, Repo,
      strategy: :keyset,
      cursor_fields: [:inserted_at, :id],
      batch_size: 50
    )

module_attributes.name: moduledoc
module_attributes.value:
A stream abstraction over Ecto queries for efficient pagination of large datasets.

Provides both offset-based and cursor-based (keyset) pagination strategies with
lazy evaluation, allowing for memory-efficient processing of large result sets.

## Key Features

- Memory-efficient streaming through large datasets
- Support for both offset and keyset pagination strategies
- Result transformation pipeline
- Telemetry integration for performance monitoring
- Automatic cleanup of resources

## Examples

### Basic Usage

    # Using offset pagination (default)
    User
    |> where([u], u.age > 30)
    |> QueryStream.new(Repo)
    |> Stream.map(&User.calculate_permissions/1)
    |> Stream.take(100)
    |> Enum.to_list()

### Using Keyset Pagination

    # More efficient for large datasets
    Post
    |> order_by([p], desc: p.inserted_at, asc: p.id)
    |> QueryStream.new(Repo, strategy: :keyset, cursor_fields: [:inserted_at, :id])
    |> Stream.reject(&Post.is_deleted?/1)
    |> Enum.each(&process_post/1)

### With Custom Transformation

    Comment
    |> preload(:user)
    |> QueryStream.new(Repo, transform: &enrich_comment/1)
    |> Enum.take(10)

- `:template_preprocessor` - Function to transform SQL before execution, defaults to `nil`

Utilities for working with SQL templates and executing raw SQL queries through Ecto repositories.

This module provides functions for:
- Loading and executing SQL from template files

- Managing transaction boundaries
- Streaming query results efficiently

- Use embedded Elixir for dynamic SQL generation

- Compose complex SQL from reusable components

```elixir
RepoHelper.execute_template(MyApp.Repo, "reports/user_activity", %{
  start_date: ~D[2023-01-01],

RepoHelper.stream_template(MyApp.Repo, "analytics/large_dataset", %{
  limit: 10_000
})
|> Stream.map(&process_row/1)
|> Stream.run()

# Execute raw SQL with named parameters
RepoHelper.execute(MyApp.Repo,
  "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email LIKE :pattern AND status = :status",
  pattern: "%@example.com",
  status: "active"
)
```

Installs the Git pre-commit hook for the project.

## Overview

This task copies the pre-commit hook script from `.git-hooks/pre-commit` to
`.git/hooks/pre-commit` and makes it executable. The pre-commit hook
ensures that:

- Staged files are automatically formatted using `mix format`.
- Linting checks are performed using `mix credo`.
- All tests pass before committing using `mix test`.

## Usage

To install the pre-commit hook, simply run:

    mix hook.install

This will ensure the hook is set up correctly for your project.

## Customization

You can modify the pre-commit hook by editing the `hooks/pre-commit` file.
After making changes, re-run `mix hook.install` to update the hook.

## Notes

- Ensure the `.git-hooks/pre-commit` file exists and is correctly configured before
  running this task.
- This task automatically sets the correct permissions for the hook.

    # Build with CUDA support
    mix llama.build --cublas

    # Build with Metal support (macOS)
    mix llama.build --metal

    # Build with specific branch/tag
    mix llama.build --branch v0.5.0

    # Clean build and rebuild
    mix llama.build --clean

Searches for models on Hugging Face or lists available files in a specific model repository.

This Mix task provides a powerful interface for discovering and exploring language models
available on Hugging Face. It can be used to search across all models or examine the contents
of a specific repository, with options for filtering, sorting, and downloading.

## Features

* Search for models across Hugging Face by name or characteristics
* List all files in a specific repository
* Filter results by format (e.g., GGUF) or parameter size
* Display detailed information about models
* Output results in JSON format for automation
* Easily download models after finding them

## Usage

    mix model.search [options] [search_term]

## Options

    --repo         - Only list files in a specific repository (e.g. TheBloke/Llama-3-8B-GGUF)
    --format       - Filter by file format (e.g. gguf, safetensors)
    --size         - Filter by parameter size (e.g. 7b, 13b)
    --limit        - Maximum number of results to show (default: 10)
    --full-info    - Show detailed information for each model
    --token        - Hugging Face API token (or set HF_TOKEN environment variable)
    --json         - Output results in JSON format
    --debug        - Show debug information including API URL
    --download     - Automatically download a file after listing (requires --repo)

## Examples

    # Search for models by name
    mix model.search llama

    # Search for models with specific characteristics
    mix model.search mistral --size 7b --format gguf

    # List all files in a specific repository
    mix model.search --repo TheBloke/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1-GGUF

    # Show more detailed information for each result
    mix model.search phi-2 --full-info --limit 5

    # Output results as JSON
    mix model.search --repo TheBloke/Mistral-7B-v0.1-GGUF --json

    # List files and download a specific one automatically
    mix model.search --repo TheBloke/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1-GGUF --download

Generate a CA certificate for the HTTPS proxy.

This task creates a new self-signed CA certificate and private key to be used
for HTTPS proxying. The certificate and key are stored in the specified path.

## Usage

    mix prismatic.certs.generate [options]

## Options

  - `--key-size`, `-k`: RSA key size in bits (default: `2048`).
  - `--validity`, `-v`: Validity period of the certificate in days
    (default: `3650` days, ~10 years).

  Subject components (optional, default values shown):
  - `--country`, `-c`: Country code (default: `US`).
  - `--state`, `-s`: State or province (default: `CA`).
  - `--locality`, `-l`: Locality or city (default: `San Francisco`).
  - `--organization`, `-o`: Organization name (default: `Prismatic`).
  - `--organizational-unit`, `-u`: Organizational unit name (default: `IT`).
  - `--common-name`, `-n`: Common name (default: `Prismatic Proxy CA`).
  - `--email-address`, `-e`: Email address (default: `admin@prismatic.com`).

## Examples

    # Generate CA certificate with default settings
    mix prismatic.certs.generate

    # Generate CA certificate with custom DN and validity
    mix prismatic.certs.generate --key-size 4096 --validity 1825 --country "DE" --state "Bavaria" --locality "Munich" --organization "Custom Org" --organizational-unit "Security" --common-name "My Proxy CA"

The generated files are stored in the `priv/certs/` directory by default.

Install the CA certificate in the trusted store.

This task installs the generated CA certificate into the system's trusted
certificate store. It requires elevated privileges (sudo) on most platforms.

## Usage

    mix prismatic.certs.install [options]

## Options

  - `--cert-path`, `-c`: Path to the CA certificate file (default: the generated certificate path).
  - `--trust-store`, `-t`: Specify the trust store to use (default: auto-detected based on OS).

## Supported Platforms

  - MacOS: Uses the `security` command.
  - Linux: Uses `update-ca-certificates` or `trust` depending on the distribution.
  - Windows: Displays instructions for manual installation.

## Examples

    # Install using the default certificate and trust store
    mix prismatic.certs.install

    # Install with a custom certificate path
    mix prismatic.certs.install --cert-path priv/certs/ca.pem

    # Specify the trust store explicitly
    mix prismatic.certs.install --trust-store macos

Comprehensive prompt management system for Prismatic.

This task provides a CLI interface to the Prismatic.Prompts module,
allowing management of prompts from the command line.

## Usage

    mix prismatic.prompts COMMAND [options]

## Commands

    list     List all available prompts
    info     Show detailed information about a prompt
    run      Run a prompt to generate code
    update   Update prompts from a remote source
    validate Validate prompt structure and metadata
    create   Create a new prompt from template
    export   Export prompts to various formats

## Examples

    # List all prompts
    mix prismatic.prompts list

    # Show info about a specific prompt
    mix prismatic.prompts info agent_creator

    # Run a prompt to generate code
    mix prismatic.prompts run agent_creator --param "name=MyAgent" --param "traits=analytical,creative"

    # Update prompts from remote
    mix prismatic.prompts update --source https://github.com/org/prompts

    # Export prompts to HTML
    mix prismatic.prompts export --format html --output prompts.html

## Options

Each command has its own set of options. Run `mix help prismatic.prompts.<command>`
for command-specific help.

module_attributes.name: moduledoc
module_attributes.value:
Updates README.md files in trait directories to reflect implementation status.

This task scans all trait directories (or a specific one), identifies which
traits have been implemented, and updates the README.md checkboxes accordingly.

The update is bidirectional:
- It checks/unchecks existing traits based on implementation status
- It adds any implemented traits that aren't already listed in the README
- It maintains strict alphabetical ordering of traits in the README

## Usage

    mix prismatic.readme.update [OPTIONS]

## Options

    * `--dir DIR` - Base traits directory (default: "lib/prismatic/traits")
    * `--type TYPE` - Only update a specific trait type (e.g., "cognitive")
    * `--dry-run` - Show what would be updated without making changes
    * `--verbose` - Show detailed information during processing
    * `--create-missing` - Create README.md files if they don't exist
    * `--unchecked-only` - Only check boxes, never uncheck them

## Examples

    # Update all README files
    mix prismatic.readme.update

    # Update only cognitive traits README
    mix prismatic.readme.update --type cognitive

    # Dry run to see what would change
    mix prismatic.readme.update --dry-run --verbose

    # Create missing README files
    mix prismatic.readme.update --create-missing

    # Only check new traits, don't uncheck any
    mix prismatic.readme.update --unchecked-only

module_attributes.name: moduledoc
module_attributes.value:
Analyzes and manages trait dependencies in the Prismatic framework.

This task examines the relationships between traits, identifying compatible and opposing
trait connections, finding missing dependencies, and generating visualizations of the
dependency graph. It can help maintain the integrity of the trait ecosystem by ensuring
dependencies are consistent and complete.

## Usage

    mix prismatic.trait.dependencies [COMMAND] [OPTIONS]

## Commands

    * `analyze` - Analyze trait dependencies (default)
    * `graph` - Generate a dependency graph visualization
    * `check` - Check for missing or inconsistent dependencies
    * `fix` - Fix inconsistent dependencies automatically

## Options

    * `--output-dir` - Directory containing traits (default: "lib/prismatic/traits")
    * `--format` - Output format for analysis (text, json, markdown, dot) (default: text)
    * `--to` - Path to output file (default: prints to console)
    * `--trait` - Focus on a specific trait (format: "type/category")
    * `--type` - Focus on a specific trait type
    * `--depth` - Maximum dependency depth to analyze (default: 2)
    * `--show-missing` - Show missing dependency implementations (default: true)
    * `--reciprocal` - Check if dependencies are reciprocal (default: true)
    * `--verify-opposing` - Verify that opposing traits aren't also compatible (default: true)
    * `--fix-missing` - During fix, create skeleton files for missing dependencies (default: false)

## Examples

    # Analyze all trait dependencies
    mix prismatic.trait.dependencies

    # Generate a GraphViz DOT file of dependencies
    mix prismatic.trait.dependencies graph --format=dot --to=traits.dot

    # Check dependencies for a specific trait
    mix prismatic.trait.dependencies check --trait=moral/compassionate_integrity

    # Fix inconsistent dependencies
    mix prismatic.trait.dependencies fix

    # Analyze with limited depth
    mix prismatic.trait.dependencies --depth=1

module_attributes.name: moduledoc
module_attributes.value:
Generates a new trait implementation for the Prismatic framework.

This Mix task uses ChatGPT to automatically generate trait implementations
based on the trait type and category provided. It creates a new Elixir module
file with a fully implemented trait following the Prismatic trait structure.

## Usage

    mix prismatic.trait.generate TRAIT_TYPE TRAIT_CATEGORY [OPTIONS]
    mix prismatic.trait.generate --yaml PATH_TO_YAML [OPTIONS]
    mix prismatic.trait.generate [--auto] [OPTIONS]
    mix prismatic.trait.generate --missing [OPTIONS]

## Arguments

    * `TRAIT_TYPE` - The type of trait (e.g., cognitive, emotional, social)
    * `TRAIT_CATEGORY` - The specific trait category (e.g., analytical, angry, diplomatic)

## Options

    * `--output-dir` - Custom output directory (default: "lib/prismatic/traits")
    * `--api-key` - OpenAI API key (alternatively set OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable)
    * `--model` - GPT model to use (default: "gpt-4o")
    * `--temperature` - Temperature for generation (default: 0.7)
    * `--force` - Overwrite existing trait file if it exists
    * `--skip` - Skip generation if file exists
    * `--fail` - Abort if file exists
    * `--yaml` - Path to YAML file containing traits to generate in batch
    * `--timeout` - API request timeout in milliseconds (default: 60000)
    * `--max-retries` - Maximum number of retries for API requests (default: 2)
    * `--recursive` - Recursively generate referenced traits if they don't exist
    * `--max-recursive-depth` - Maximum depth for recursive trait generation (default: 3)
    * `--template` - Path to template file for generating traits
    * `--auto` - Auto-discover missing traits from existing files
    * `--missing` - Find and generate traits directly referenced but missing
    * `--limit` - Maximum number of traits to generate (default: 10)
    * `--update-readme` - Update the README.md with newly generated traits (default: true)
    * `--no-update-readme` - Don't update README.md files
    * `--verbose-readme` - Show detailed information during README updates
    * `--dry-run` - Show what would be generated without making actual API calls
    * `--save-history` - Save generated trait prompts and responses to a history file (useful for auditing)
    * `--history-dir` - Directory to save generation history (default: ".prismatic_history")
    * `--format` - Format generated code with "mix format" after generation (default: true)
    * `--no-format` - Skip code formatting
    * `--validate` - Validate generated traits by compiling them (default: true)
    * `--no-validate` - Skip validation
    * `--batch-sleep` - Milliseconds to sleep between batch requests (default: 1000)
    * `--override` - Override specific values in the trait template (format: key=value,key2=value2)
    * `--parallel` - Generate multiple traits in parallel (WARNING: can trigger rate limits)
    * `--interactive` - Run in interactive mode with step by step guidance

## Template File

You can create a template file to customize trait generation. The template supports
the following placeholders:

* `{{module_name}}` - Full module name (e.g., Prismatic.Traits.Cognitive.Analytical)
* `{{trait_type}}` - Trait type (e.g., cognitive)
* `{{trait_category}}` - Trait category in snake_case (e.g., abstract_thinking)
* `{{capitalized_category}}` - Trait category with first letter capitalized (e.g., Abstract_thinking)

## Examples

    # Generate a cognitive analytical trait
    mix prismatic.trait.generate cognitive analytical

    # Generate a social diplomatic trait using a specific model
    mix prismatic.trait.generate social diplomatic --model gpt-4o --temperature 0.5

    # Generate to a custom directory with custom filename
    mix prismatic.trait.generate emotional cheerful --output-dir lib/custom/traits

    # Generate multiple traits from a YAML file with increased timeout and retries
    mix prismatic.trait.generate --yaml config/traits.yaml --timeout 120000 --max-retries 3

    # Generate a trait and recursively generate all referenced traits
    mix prismatic.trait.generate cognitive abstract_thinking --recursive

    # Generate a trait but don't update the README
    mix prismatic.trait.generate cognitive analytical --no-update-readme

    # Generate a trait and update the README with verbose output
    mix prismatic.trait.generate cognitive analytical --verbose-readme

    # Dry run to see what would be generated
    mix prismatic.trait.generate cognitive analytical --dry-run

    # Override specific values in the trait template
    mix prismatic.trait.generate cognitive analytical --override base_strength=75,trait_description="Custom description"

    # Generate traits in interactive mode
    mix prismatic.trait.generate --interactive

This task allows you to update specific fields in an existing trait without

## Usage

## Arguments

    * `TRAIT_TYPE` - The type of trait (e.g., cognitive, emotional, moral)
    * `TRAIT_CATEGORY` - The specific trait category (e.g., analytical, angry, compassionate_integrity)

## Options

    * `--description` - Update the trait description

    * `--remove-compatible` - Remove a compatible trait (format: "Type.Category")
    * `--add-opposing` - Add an opposing trait (format: "Type.Category")
    * `--remove-opposing` - Remove an opposing trait (format: "Type.Category")
    * `--add-aspect` - Add an influence aspect (format: ":aspect_name")

    * `--update-state` - Update a state value (format: "state_key:0.XX")
    * `--dry-run` - Show changes without writing to file
    * `--backup` - Create a backup of the original file before updating

    mix prismatic.trait.update moral compassionate_integrity --add-compatible="Emotional.Kindness"

    mix prismatic.trait.update moral compassionate_integrity --update-state="moral_reasoning:0.9"

    mix prismatic.trait.update moral compassionate_integrity --base-strength=80 --add-aspect=":fairness" --remove-compatible="Cognitive.Rigidity"

Manages trait versioning.

This task allows you to view, update, and manage trait versions, ensuring proper
versioning of trait implementations.

## Usage

    mix prismatic.trait.version [COMMAND] [OPTIONS]

## Commands

    * `list` - List version information for traits (default)
    * `update` - Update version for a trait or traits
    * `check` - Check for version inconsistencies
    * `set-default` - Set default version for new traits

## Options

    * `--trait` - Specific trait to manage (format: "type/category")
    * `--type` - Filter to a specific trait type
    * `--old` - Current version to match (for update)
    * `--new` - New version to set
    * `--all` - Apply to all matching traits
    * `--output-dir` - Directory containing traits (default: "lib/prismatic/traits")
    * `--format` - Output format for listing (text, json, csv) (default: text)
    * `--force` - Force version update without confirmation

## Examples

    # List versions for all traits
    mix prismatic.trait.version list

    # List versions for cognitive traits
    mix prismatic.trait.version list --type=cognitive

    # Update version for a specific trait
    mix prismatic.trait.version update --trait=moral/compassionate_integrity --new=1.1.0

    # Update version for all traits
    mix prismatic.trait.version update --all --old=1.0.0 --new=1.1.0

    # Check for version inconsistencies
    mix prismatic.trait.version check

    # Set default version for new traits
    mix prismatic.trait.version set-default --new=1.1.0

Checks if the token is valid and returns its underlying lookup query.

The query returns the user found by the token, if any.

This is used to validate requests to change the user
email. It is different from `verify_email_token_query/2` precisely because
`verify_email_token_query/2` validates the email has not changed, which is
the starting point by this function.

The given token is valid if it matches its hashed counterpart in the
database and if it has not expired (after @change_email_validity_in_days).
The context must always start with "change:".

module_attributes.name: doc
module_attributes.value:
Checks if the token is valid and returns its underlying lookup query.

The query returns the user found by the token, if any.

The given token is valid if it matches its hashed counterpart in the
database and the user email has not changed. This function also checks
if the token is being used within a certain period, depending on the
context. The default contexts supported by this function are either
"confirm", for account confirmation emails, and "reset_password",
for resetting the password. For verifying requests to change the email,
see `verify_change_email_token_query/2`.

module_attributes.name: doc
module_attributes.value:
Builds a token and its hash to be delivered to the user's email.

The non-hashed token is sent to the user email while the
hashed part is stored in the database. The original token cannot be reconstructed,
which means anyone with read-only access to the database cannot directly use
the token in the application to gain access. Furthermore, if the user changes
their email in the system, the tokens sent to the previous email are no longer
valid.

Users can easily adapt the existing code to provide other types of delivery methods,
for example, by phone numbers.

module_attributes.name: doc
module_attributes.value:
Checks if the token is valid and returns its underlying lookup query.

The query returns the user found by the token, if any.

The token is valid if it matches the value in the database and it has
not expired (after @session_validity_in_days).

module_attributes.name: doc
module_attributes.value:
Generates a token that will be stored in a signed place,
such as session or cookie. As they are signed, those
tokens do not need to be hashed.

The reason why we store session tokens in the database, even
though Phoenix already provides a session cookie, is because
Phoenix' default session cookies are not persisted, they are
simply signed and potentially encrypted. This means they are
valid indefinitely, unless you change the signing/encryption
salt.

Therefore, storing them allows individual user
sessions to be expired. The token system can also be extended
to store additional data, such as the device used for logging in.
You could then use this information to display all valid sessions
and devices in the UI and allow users to explicitly expire any
session they deem invalid.

Finds and obtains information about CDP-compatible browsers on the system.

This module searches for CDP-compatible browsers in a configurable and platform-compliant way.
It supports macOS and Linux, searching for various binary name variants and resolving `.app` bundles on macOS.

## Configuration

Configure `Prismatic.Browsers.BrowserFinder` using the application environment:

    config :prismatic, Prismatic.Browsers.BrowserFinder,
      paths: [
        "~/.local/bin",
        "/usr/bin",
        "/usr/local/bin",
        "/Applications"
      ],
      binaries: [
        "brave-browsersbrowsers",
        "chromium",
        "firefox",
        "google-chrome",
        "google-chrome-stable",
        "microsoft-edge",
        "playwright",
        "vivaldi",
      ],
      mac_app_bundles: [
        "/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome",
        "/Applications/Chromium.app/Contents/MacOS/Chromium",
        "/Applications/Brave Browser.app/Contents/MacOS/Brave Browser",
        "/Applications/Firefox.app/Contents/MacOS/firefox",
        "/Applications/Vivaldi.app/Contents/MacOS/Vivaldi",
        "/Applications/Microsoft Edge.app/Contents/MacOS/Microsoft Edge"
      ]

## Examples

    iex> Prismatic.Browsers.BrowserFinder.find_browsers()
    [
      %{
        id: "c4ca4238a0b923820dcc509a6f75849b",
        name: "chromium",
        path: "/usr/bin/chromium",
        version: "104.0.5112.81",
        compatible: true
      },
      %{
        id: "81dc9bdb52d04dc20036dbd8313ed055",
        name: "google-chrome",
        path: "/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome",
        version: "99.0.4844.51",
        compatible: true
      }
    ]

A GenServer-based worker for managing a Playwright browser instance.

This module is designed to manage a single Playwright browser instance, with support for
distributed supervision using `Horde.Registry`. It provides functionalities to:

- Start a new browser worker identified by a unique name.
- Retrieve the current state of the worker.
- Ensure safe shutdown of the Playwright browser instance.

## Example Usage

    iex> {:ok, _pid} = Prismatic.Browsers.BrowserWorker.start_link(name: "browser_worker_1")
    ...> state = Prismatic.Browsers.BrowserWorker.get_state("browser_worker_1")
    ...> Map.get(state, :name)
    "browser_worker_1"

module_attributes.name: moduledoc
module_attributes.value:
The `Prismatic.Cluster` module is a core part of the Prismatic application, providing functionality for monitoring, managing, and interacting with a distributed cluster of nodes. It integrates with Ash, Phoenix PubSub, and Horde to achieve cluster-wide coordination and scalability.

---

## Overview

### Key Responsibilities
- **Node Membership Monitoring**: Automatically detects when nodes join (`:nodeup`) or leave (`:nodedown`) the cluster.
- **Cluster Process Management**: Leverages Horde for distributed supervision and registry.
- **Node Metadata Management**: Provides APIs for retrieving and updating node metadata.
- **Inter-Service Communication**: Utilizes Phoenix PubSub for real-time event broadcasting.

---

## Architecture Diagram

### Components and Their Relationships

```mermaid
graph TD
subgraph Cluster Management
  A[Prismatic.Cluster]
  A --> B[Phoenix.PubSub]
  A --> C[Horde.Registry]
  A --> D[Horde.DynamicSupervisor]
end

subgraph Node Management
  C --> E[Node Metadata Management]
  D --> F[Distributed Process Supervision]
end

subgraph UI Integration
  B --> G[Phoenix.LiveView]
  E --> G
end

B --> H[Broadcast :nodeup and :nodedown]
D --> I[Supervise Node Processes]
```

Represents a node in the Prismatic cluster.

This module uses the Ash framework to define a resource for managing cluster nodes.
It supports operations such as retrieving, listing, and updating node status.

## Attributes
- `:id` - The unique UUID for the node.
- `:name` - The name of the node, must be a non-empty string.
- `:status` - The status of the node, can be `:connected` or `:disconnected`.

## Actions
- `:list` - Retrieves a list of all nodes.
- `:change_status` - Updates the status of a node.

## Examples

    # Listing nodes and updating a node's status
    iex> {:ok, nodes} = Prismatic.Cluster.Node.list()
    ...> node = Enum.find(nodes, &(&1.name == "node1"))
    ...> {:ok, updated_node} = Prismatic.Cluster.Node.change_status(node, :disconnected)
    ...> updated_node.status
    :disconnected

    # Checking if a node is the current node
    iex> node = %Prismatic.Cluster.Node{name: Node.self() |> Atom.to_string()}
    ...> Prismatic.Cluster.Node.self_node?(node)
    {:ok, true}

    iex> node = %Prismatic.Cluster.Node{name: "another_node"}
    ...> Prismatic.Cluster.Node.self_node?(node)
    {:ok, false}

    # Retrieving a node by ID or name
    iex> {:ok, node} = Prismatic.Cluster.Node.get(id: "some-uuid")
    ...> node.name
    "node1"

    iex> {:ok, node} = Prismatic.Cluster.Node.get(name: "node1")
    ...> node.status
    :connected

Creates a new agent and starts it as a GenServer process.

This is a convenience function that combines creating and starting
an agent in a single call. It accepts various formats for specifying
the LLM client.

## Client Specification Formats

* `{provider_module, config}` - Tuple with provider module and config
* `client_instance` - Already initialized client struct
* `:provider_name` - Atom representing a provider (requires config)
* `[provider_name: config]` - Provider name with config in keyword list
* `%{provider: provider_name, config: config}` - Map with provider and config

* `:id` - Unique identifier for the agent (optional, will be generated if not provided)
* `:name` - Human-readable name for the agent (optional)
* `:system_message` - Initial system message (optional)
* `:storage` - Storage module for persistence (optional)
* `:config` - Configuration (only needed when using provider name)

## Returns
  * `{:ok, pid}` - The pid of the agent GenServer
  * `{:error, reason}` - If the agent could not be started

## Examples

    # Using a provider atom with config
    {:ok, agent} = Prismatic.LLM.Agent.new(:chatgpt, id: "joe", config: %{api_key: System.get_env("OPENAI_API_KEY")})

    # Using an existing client
    client = Prismatic.LLM.client(:chatgpt, %{api_key: "sk-..."})
    {:ok, agent} = Prismatic.LLM.Agent.new(client, id: "joe")

    # Using a provider module tuple
    {:ok, agent} = Prismatic.LLM.Agent.new({Prismatic.LLM.Clients.ChatGPT, %{api_key: System.get_env("OPENAI_API_KEY")}}, id: "joe")

    # Using keyword list format
    {:ok, agent} = Prismatic.LLM.Agent.new([chatgpt: %{api_key: System.get_env("OPENAI_API_KEY")}], id: "joe")

    # Using map format
    {:ok, agent} = Prismatic.LLM.Agent.new(%{provider: :chatgpt, config: %{api_key: System.get_env("OPENAI_API_KEY")}}, id: "joe")

Deletes an agent's saved state by ID.

This function should remove the stored state of an agent with the given ID.
If the agent cannot be found, it should still return `:ok` to indicate that
the agent state no longer exists.

## Parameters
  * `id` - The unique identifier for the agent

## Returns
  * `:ok` - If the delete was successful
  * `{:error, reason}` - If the delete failed

## Examples

```elixir
# Implementing the delete callback
@impl true
def delete(id) do
  # Convert ID to string for consistency
  id_str = to_string(id)

  # Delete the agent data
  case MyDatabase.delete(id_str) do
    :ok -> :ok
    {:error, :not_found} -> :ok  # Consider it deleted if not found
    {:error, reason} -> {:error, "Failed to delete agent: #{reason}"}
  end
end
```

Loads the agent's client state by ID.

This function is responsible for retrieving and deserializing the state of an
LLM client associated with an agent. If the agent cannot be found, it should
return an error.

## Parameters
  * `id` - The unique identifier for the agent

## Returns
  * `{:ok, client}` - If the load was successful
  * `{:error, reason}` - If the load failed

## Examples

```elixir
# Implementing the load callback
@impl true
def load(id) do
  # Convert ID to string for consistency
  id_str = to_string(id)

  # Retrieve the serialized data
  case MyDatabase.get(id_str) do
    {:ok, serialized} ->
      # Deserialize the client
      try do
        client = :erlang.binary_to_term(serialized)
        {:ok, client}
      rescue
        e -> {:error, "Failed to deserialize agent: #{inspect(e)}"}
      end

    {:error, :not_found} ->
      {:error, "Agent with ID #{id_str} not found"}

    {:error, reason} ->
      {:error, "Failed to load agent: #{reason}"}
  end
end
```

module_attributes.name: moduledoc
module_attributes.value:
Behaviour defining the interface for LLM agent storage backends.

Storage backends are responsible for persisting and retrieving agent state.
Implementations can use various persistence mechanisms like memory, files,
or databases.

## Available Storage Implementations

* `Prismatic.LLM.Agent.Storage.Memory` - In-memory storage using ETS
* `Prismatic.LLM.Agent.Storage.File` - File-based storage with serialization
* `Prismatic.LLM.Agent.Storage.ETF` - External Term Format storage (efficient binary serialization)
* `Prismatic.LLM.Agent.Storage.Composite` - Combines multiple storage backends

## Creating a Custom Storage Backend

To create a custom storage backend, implement the required callbacks:

```elixir
defmodule MyApp.CustomStorage do
  @behaviour Prismatic.LLM.Agent.Storage

  @impl true
  def save(id, client) do
    # Implementation to save state
    :ok
  end

  @impl true
  def load(id) do
    # Implementation to load state
    {:ok, client}
  end

  @impl true
  def list() do
    # Implementation to list all agents
    {:ok, ["agent1", "agent2"]}
  end

  @impl true
  def delete(id) do
    # Implementation to delete state
    :ok
  end
end
```

## Usage in Agents

Storage backends can be specified when creating an agent:

```elixir
# Using memory storage
memory_storage = Prismatic.LLM.Agent.Storage.Memory

{:ok, agent} = Agent.start_link(
  id: "joe",
  provider: :chatgpt,
  config: [api_key: "sk-..."],
  storage: memory_storage
)
```

## Choosing the Right Storage Backend

The choice of storage backend depends on your requirements:

* **Memory** - Fast but non-persistent (loses data on restart)
* **File** - Persistent but slower
* **ETF** - Persistent with efficient serialization
* **Composite** - Combines advantages of multiple backends (e.g., memory for speed + file for persistence)

## Storage Strategies

For advanced use cases, consider these strategies:

* **Cache with Backup** - Memory (primary) + File (secondary) with cascade reads
* **Write-Through Cache** - Memory + File with write-all strategy
* **High Availability** - Multiple distributed storage backends

Creates a new composite storage with the given backends.

## Options
  * `:backends` - List of storage backends in priority order (required)
  * `:read_strategy` - Either `:first_available` or `:cascade` (default: `:first_available`)
  * `:write_strategy` - Either `:all` or `:primary_only` (default: `:all`)

## Read strategies:
  * `:first_available` - Return the first successful result from any backend
  * `:cascade` - Try each backend in order, updating previous backends with found data

## Write strategies:
  * `:all` - Write to all backends
  * `:primary_only` - Write only to the first backend

## Returns
  * A new composite storage struct

## Examples

    iex> memory = Prismatic.LLM.Agent.Storage.Memory
    ...> file = Prismatic.LLM.Agent.Storage.File.new(directory: "/tmp")
    ...> composite = Prismatic.LLM.Agent.Storage.Composite.new(backends: [memory, file])
    ...> composite.read_strategy
    :first_available
    iex> composite.write_strategy
    :all

    iex> composite =
    ...>   Prismatic.LLM.Agent.Storage.Composite.new(
    ...>     backends: [memory, file],
    ...>     read_strategy: :cascade,
    ...>     write_strategy: :primary_only
    ...>   )
    ...> 
    ...> composite.read_strategy
    :cascade
    iex> composite.write_strategy
    :primary_only

module_attributes.name: moduledoc
module_attributes.value:
External Term Format (ETF) storage implementation for LLM agent state.

This module provides a persistent storage mechanism using Erlang's External Term Format.
Agent states are serialized using `:erlang.term_to_binary/1` and stored in individual
files with the `.etf` extension. This is more efficient than using standard File storage
as it preserves Elixir/Erlang data types without needing to implement custom serialization.

## Advantages

* **Native Erlang Serialization** - Preserves all Elixir/Erlang data types
* **Good Performance** - Fast serialization and deserialization
* **Memory Efficient** - Only loads agents when requested
* **Compatibility** - Works with complex struct types
* **Persistence** - Survives application restarts

## Usage

```elixir
# Create an ETF storage with a custom directory
etf_storage = Prismatic.LLM.Agent.Storage.ETF.new(directory: "/path/to/storage")

# Start an agent with ETF storage
{:ok, agent} = Agent.start_link(
  id: "joe",
  provider: :chatgpt,
  config: [api_key: "sk-..."],
  storage: etf_storage
)
```

## Security Considerations

ETF files contain serialized Erlang terms. When deserializing terms from untrusted sources,
there is a potential security risk. This storage backend should only be used with files
that your application has created, in directories that are properly secured against
unauthorized access.

Sets the client specification for the agent.

This function accepts the same client specification formats as `Agent.new/2`:

## Client Specification Formats

* `{provider_module, config}` - Tuple with provider module and config
* `client_instance` - Already initialized client struct
* `:provider_name` - Atom representing a provider (requires config)
* `[provider_name: config]` - Provider name with config in keyword list
* `%{provider: provider_name, config: config}` - Map with provider and config

The configuration can be provided separately in the builder chain using
`with_options/2` when using the provider name format.

## Parameters
  * `builder` - The builder struct
  * `provider` - The LLM provider name
  * `config` - The configuration for the provider

## Returns
  * Updated builder with the client specification set

## Examples

    iex> builder =
    ...>   Prismatic.LLM.AgentBuilder.new()
    ...>   |> Prismatic.LLM.AgentBuilder.with_client(:chatgpt, %{api_key: "sk-..."})
    ...> 
    ...> {provider, _config} = builder.client_spec
    ...> provider
    :chatgpt

Subscribes the current process to updates in a specific area.

The subscribed process will receive messages in the format:
`{:blackboard_update, area, {:update, key, value}}` when an entry is added or updated.
`{:blackboard_update, area, {:delete, key}}` when an entry is deleted.
`{:blackboard_update, area, :clear}` when an area is cleared.

## Parameters
  * `blackboard` - The blackboard process or name
  * `area` - The knowledge area to subscribe to
  * `opts` - Additional options:
    * `:timeout` - Call timeout in milliseconds (default: 5000)
    * `:retry` - Number of retry attempts for transient errors (default: 3)

## Returns
  * `:ok` - If the subscription was successful
  * `{:error, reason}` - If the subscription failed

## Examples

    # Subscribe to the "queries" area
    Prismatic.LLM.Blackboard.subscribe(blackboard, "queries")

    # Later in the process...
    receive do
      {:blackboard_update, "queries", {:update, query_id, query}} ->
        # Handle the new query
    end

## Options

  * `:channel_options` - Options for the notification channel (default: `%{}`)
  * `:storage` - Storage backend module (default: `Prismatic.LLM.Blackboard.Storage.Mnesia`)
  * `:storage_options` - Options for the storage backend (default: `%{}`)
  * `:max_area_size` - Maximum number of entries in an area (default: 10,000)
  * `:ttl_check_interval` - Interval in ms for checking TTL expirations (optional)

## Returns
  * `{:ok, pid}` - The PID of the blackboard process
  * `{:error, reason}` - If the blackboard could not be started

## Examples

    # Start with default settings
    {:ok, blackboard} = Prismatic.LLM.Blackboard.start_link()

    # Start with a registered name and custom modules
    {:ok, blackboard} = Prismatic.LLM.Blackboard.start_link(
      name: MyApp.Blackboard,
      channel: MyApp.CustomChannel,
      channel_options: %{some_option: true},
      storage: MyApp.CustomStorage,
      storage_options: %{path: "/path/to/data"}
    )

module_attributes.name: moduledoc
module_attributes.value:
A central blackboard for sharing knowledge between LLM agents and knowledge sources.

This module implements a blackboard architectural pattern where multiple specialized
components (knowledge sources) can collaborate by sharing information through a
central repository (the blackboard).

The blackboard is organized into "areas" which are like sections or categories
of knowledge. Each area contains key-value pairs. Components can subscribe to
specific areas to be notified of changes.

## Features

* Organized knowledge with area-based categorization
* Pluggable notification channels for publishing changes
* Pluggable storage backends for persistence
* Support for transient and persistent knowledge

## Example Usage

```elixir
# Start a blackboard with default settings
{:ok, blackboard} = Prismatic.LLM.Blackboard.start_link()

# Write some knowledge
Prismatic.LLM.Blackboard.write(blackboard, "facts", "elixir_creator", "José Valim")

# Read knowledge
{:ok, creator} = Prismatic.LLM.Blackboard.read(blackboard, "facts", "elixir_creator")
# => {:ok, "José Valim"}

# Subscribe to an area
Prismatic.LLM.Blackboard.subscribe(blackboard, "facts")
```

Behavior defining the interface for blackboard notification channels.

Notification channels are responsible for publishing updates and handling
subscriptions when blackboard data changes. Implementations can use
various mechanisms like PubSub, RabbitMQ, etc.

## Creating a Custom Channel

To create a custom notification channel, implement the required callbacks:


module_attributes.value:
Mnesia-based storage implementation for the blackboard.

This module provides persistent storage for blackboard data using Mnesia,
which offers transactional, distributed, and fault-tolerant capabilities.

## Options

* `:table_name` - The Mnesia table name to use (default: `:prismatic_blackboard`)
* `:nodes` - List of nodes to replicate data to (default: `[node()]`)
* `:type` - Table type, `:set`, `:ordered_set`, or `:bag` (default: `:set`)
* `:disc_copies` - Nodes with disc copies (default: `[node()]`)
* `:ram_copies` - Nodes with RAM-only copies (default: `[]`)

## Example Usage

```elixir
# Start a blackboard with Mnesia storage
{:ok, blackboard} = Prismatic.LLM.Blackboard.start_link(
  storage: Prismatic.LLM.Blackboard.Storage.Mnesia,
  storage_options: %{
    table_name: :my_blackboard,
    disc_copies: [node()]
  }
)
```

## Requirements

Mnesia must be started before using this storage backend. You can ensure this
by adding the following to your application startup:

```elixir
# In your application.ex
def start(_type, _args) do
  # Start Mnesia
  :mnesia.start()

  # Create schema if it doesn't exist
  if :mnesia.system_info(:use_dir) == false do
    :mnesia.create_schema([node()])
    :mnesia.start()
  end

  # Rest of your application startup...
end
```

Top-level interface for invoking LLM clients via structured prompts.

This module accepts `Prismatic.LLM.Prompt` structs and dispatches them to the
appropriate backend implementation based on the model prefix. It wraps the result
in a unified `Prismatic.LLM.Response` struct and handles common error normalization.

## Responsibilities

- Normalize interaction with heterogeneous LLM clients (Claude, Llama, LM Studio, ChatGPT)
- Provide fallback-friendly and pluggable dispatch logic
- Serve as the default entry point for anything that wants to call an LLM in Prismatic

## Supported model prefixes

  - "claude"     => Prismatic.LLM.Clients.Claude
  - "llama"      => Prismatic.LLM.Clients.Llama
  - "gpt-"       => Prismatic.LLM.Clients.ChatGPT
  - "lmstudio"   => Prismatic.LLM.Clients.LMStudio

## Example

    iex> prompt =
    ...>   Prismatic.LLM.Prompt.new(:fallacy_check, "All birds fly. Penguins are birds. So...",
    ...>     model: "llama-3-8b"
    ...>   )
    ...> 
    ...> Prismatic.LLM.Dispatcher.call(prompt)
    %Prismatic.LLM.Response{status: :ok, output: "...", model: "llama-3-8b", ...}

module_attributes.value:
Behavior defining the interface for blackboard knowledge sources.

Knowledge sources are specialized components that contribute to problem solving
by reading from and writing to the blackboard. Each knowledge source provides
specific expertise in certain domains.

## Creating a Custom Knowledge Source

To create a custom knowledge source, implement the required callbacks:

```elixir
defmodule MyApp.WeatherKnowledgeSource do
  @behaviour Prismatic.LLM.KnowledgeSource

  @impl true
  def init(blackboard, options) do
    # Initialize the knowledge source
    # Subscribe to relevant blackboard areas
    Prismatic.LLM.Blackboard.subscribe(blackboard, "queries")
    {:ok, %{blackboard: blackboard, options: options}}
  end

  @impl true
  def process_update(blackboard, area, update, state) do
    case update do
      {:update, key, query} when area == "queries" ->
        if weather_related?(query) do
          weather_data = fetch_weather_data(query)
          Prismatic.LLM.Blackboard.write(blackboard, "weather", key, weather_data)
        end

      _ ->
        # Ignore other updates
    end

    {:ok, state}
  end

  @impl true
  def terminate(state) do
    # Clean up resources
    :ok
  end

  # Helper functions
  defp weather_related?(query) do
    # ...
  end

  defp fetch_weather_data(query) do
    # ...
  end
end
```

module_attributes.name: moduledoc
module_attributes.value:
A helper module for constructing Lean source code from Elixir.

## Purpose

This module provides a composable and structured way to build `.lean` source code from Elixir data.
It is designed for agents or runtime components that need to:

- Generate minimal Lean theorems
- Vary tactic style (e.g. `simp`, `induction`, `cases`, `super`)
- Compose proof goals with dynamic parameters
- Support Lean invocation through `LeanBridge`

## Example

    iex> script = Prismatic.LLM.LeanScript.new("n = n")
    ...> Prismatic.LLM.LeanScript.render(script)
    "import Init

theorem auto_proof (n : Nat) : n = n := by simp"

## Use in practice

This module is typically used with `LeanBridge.run/1`:

    script = LeanScript.new("n = n")
    {:ok, bundle} = LeanBridge.run(LeanScript.render(script))
    assert bundle.verified == true

module_attributes.name: moduledoc
module_attributes.value:
Behavior and utilities for agent middleware.

Middleware allows intercepting and modifying agent operations at different
points in their lifecycle. This enables features like logging, content filtering,
and transformations without modifying the core agent code.

## Lifecycle Hooks

Middleware can implement one or more of the following hooks:

* `init/1` - Called when the middleware is initialized
* `before_init/3` - Called before agent initialization
* `after_init/3` - Called after agent initialization
* `before_ask/3` - Called before processing a user query
* `after_ask/3` - Called after processing a user query
* `before_system/3` - Called before setting a system message
* `after_system/3` - Called after setting a system message
* `before_reset/3` - Called before resetting the conversation
* `after_reset/3` - Called after resetting the conversation
* `before_save/3` - Called before saving agent state
* `after_save/3` - After saving agent state
* `before_load/3` - Before loading agent state
* `after_load/3` - After loading agent state

All hooks are optional. Implement only the ones you need.

## Example Implementation

```elixir
defmodule MyApp.LoggingMiddleware do
  @behaviour Prismatic.LLM.Middleware

  @impl true
  def init(options) do
    log_level = Map.get(options, :level, :info)
    {:ok, %{level: log_level}}
  end

  @impl true
  def before_ask(agent_state, context, mw_state) do
    {agent_state, context, mw_state}
  end

  @impl true
  def after_ask(agent_state, context, mw_state) do
    {agent_state, context, mw_state}
  end
end
```

## Usage with Agents

Middleware is typically added through the agent builder:

```elixir
{:ok, agent} = Prismatic.LLM.AgentBuilder.new()
  |> Prismatic.LLM.AgentBuilder.with_middleware(MyApp.LoggingMiddleware, %{level: :info})
  |> Prismatic.LLM.AgentBuilder.build()
```

## Middleware Order

The order of middleware matters. Middleware is applied in the order it's added:

```elixir
# First content is filtered, then responses are truncated
builder
  |> middleware(Prismatic.LLM.Middleware.ContentFilter, %{})
  |> middleware(Prismatic.LLM.Middleware.ResponseTransformer, %{max_length: 200})
```

## Error Handling

It's important to handle errors gracefully in middleware to avoid crashing the agent:

```elixir
@impl true
def before_ask(agent_state, context, mw_state) do
  try
    # Risky operation here
    {agent_state, context, mw_state}
  rescue
    e ->
      # Return original state and context on error
      {agent_state, context, mw_state}
  end
end
```

A middleware that filters content for sensitive or inappropriate material.

This middleware inspects messages sent to and responses received from the LLM,
and can modify or reject them based on filtering rules.

## Options

* `:level` - Filter level: `:none`, `:mild`, `:moderate`, or `:strict` (default: `:moderate`)
* `:blocked_words` - List of words to block (default: `[]`)
* `:replacement` - String to replace blocked words with (default: `"[redacted]"`)

## Example Usage

```elixir
# Add content filter middleware to an agent
{:ok, agent} = Prismatic.LLM.AgentBuilder.new()
  |> Prismatic.LLM.AgentBuilder.with_middleware(Prismatic.LLM.Middleware.ContentFilter, %{
    level: :moderate,
    blocked_words: ["inappropriate", "offensive"]
  })
  |> Prismatic.LLM.AgentBuilder.build()
```

A middleware that transforms responses from the LLM.

This middleware can apply various transformations to the LLM's responses,
such as formatting, shortening, or enhancing them.

## Options

* `:transformations` - List of transformation functions to apply (default: `[]`)
* `:simplify` - Whether to simplify responses (default: `false`)
* `:max_length` - Maximum response length (default: `nil`)

## Example Usage

```elixir
# Add response transformer middleware to an agent
{:ok, agent} = Prismatic.LLM.AgentBuilder.new()
  |> Prismatic.LLM.AgentBuilder.with_middleware(Prismatic.LLM.Middleware.ResponseTransformer, %{
    transformations: [
      &String.trim/1,
      fn text -> "✨ " <> text <> " ✨" end
    ],
    max_length: 200
  })
  |> Prismatic.LLM.AgentBuilder.build()
```

module_attributes.name: moduledoc
module_attributes.value:
Main interface for working with prompts in the Prismatic system.

This module provides high-level functions for managing and using prompts,
which are templates for code generation that integrate with LLM APIs.

## Design Philosophy

This module is designed to work equally well from:
- Command line (mix tasks)
- Phoenix LiveView components
- Other Elixir modules

All functions return predictable results that can be easily handled in
different contexts.

## Basic Usage

    # List all available prompts
    prompts = Prismatic.Prompts.list_prompts()

    # Find a specific prompt
    prompt = Prismatic.Prompts.find_prompt("agent_creator")

    # Generate code from a prompt
    {:ok, code} = Prismatic.Prompts.generate("agent_creator", %{
      "name" => "MyAgent",
      "traits" => ["analytical", "creative"]
    })

## CLI Example

    # In a mix task
    def run(args) do
      case Prismatic.Prompts.generate(prompt_name, params) do
        {:ok, code} ->
          IO.puts("Code generated successfully")
          File.write!(output_path, code)
        {:error, error_reason} ->
          Mix.shell().error("Failed: #{error_reason}")
          exit({:shutdown, 1})
      end
    end

## LiveView Example

    # In a LiveView component
    def handle_event("generate", %{"prompt" => name, "params" => params}, socket) do
      case Prismatic.Prompts.generate(name, params) do
        {:ok, code} ->
          {:noreply, assign(socket, generated_code: code, error: nil)}
        {:error, error_reason} ->
          {:noreply, assign(socket, error: error_reason)}
      end
    end

Loads all prompts from the filesystem and applies optional filtering and sorting.

module_attributes.value:
Handles loading and parsing of prompt files from the filesystem.

This module is responsible for:
- Finding prompt files in the configured directory
- Parsing YAML frontmatter and markdown content
- Applying filters and sorting
- Providing both eager and lazy loading options

## Configuration

The prompts directory can be configured in your `config.exs`:

    config :prismatic, :prompts_dir, "custom/prompts/path"

## File Structure

Prompt files should have:
- YAML frontmatter between `---` markers
- Markdown content after the frontmatter

Example:

    ---
    description: Creates a new agent
    version: 1.0.0
    author: Alice
    tags: agent, creation
    ---
    
    # Agent Creator
    
    Create an agent with name: {{name}}

## Performance Considerations

For large collections of prompts, use the `stream/1` function to avoid
loading all files into memory at once.

Renders a template with the given parameters.

Handles various parameter types and applies appropriate formatting.

## Parameter Types

- String: Inserted as-is
- Number: Converted to string
- List: Joined with commas
- Map: Pretty-printed as JSON
- Boolean: Converted to "true" or "false"
- Nil: Converted to empty string

## Examples

    iex> Template.render("Name: {{name}}", %{"name" => "Alice"})
    "Name: Alice"
    
    iex> Template.render("Count: {{count}}", %{"count" => 42})
    "Count: 42"
    
    iex> Template.render("List: {{items}}", %{"items" => [1, 2, 3]})
    "List: 1, 2, 3"

Handles template rendering and parameter interpolation for prompts.

This module provides functionality to:
- Replace parameter placeholders with values
- Format different data types appropriately
- Handle conditional logic in templates
- Process loops and iterations

## Template Syntax

- Parameters: `{{param_name}}`
- Conditionals: `{{#if condition}}...{{/if}}`
- Loops: `{{#each items}}...{{/each}}`
- Partials: `{{> partial_name}}`

## Examples

    # Simple parameter substitution
    iex> Template.render("Hello {{name}}!", %{"name" => "Alice"})
    "Hello Alice!"
    
    # Array formatting
    iex> Template.render("Traits: {{traits}}", %{"traits" => ["happy", "smart"]})
    "Traits: happy, smart"
    
    # Object formatting
    iex> Template.render("Config: {{config}}", %{"config" => %{"key" => "value"}})
    "Config: {\n  \"key\": \"value\"\n}"

Updates prompts from a remote source.

## Options

  * `:source` - Source URL or path (defaults to configured source)
  * `:force` - Force overwrite existing files (defaults to false)
  * `:dry_run` - Show what would be done without making changes
  * `:backup` - Create backups before overwriting (defaults to true)

## Examples

    # Update from default source
    iex> Updater.update()
    {:ok, 5}

    # Update from specific source with force
    iex> Updater.update(source: "https://github.com/org/prompts", force: true)

    # Dry run to see changes
    iex> Updater.update(dry_run: true)

Updates prompts from remote sources.

This module provides functionality to:
- Download prompts from various sources (Git, HTTP, local)
- Detect changes between local and remote prompts
- Apply updates with conflict resolution
- Create backups before updates

## Supported Sources

- Git repositories (via URLs containing `github.com` or other Git hosts)
- HTTP/HTTPS URLs (for direct downloads)
- Local filesystem directories

## Configuration

Set the default source in your `config.exs`:

    config :prismatic, :prompts_source, "https://github.com/prismatic-ai/prompts"

## Usage Examples

    # Update from default source
    {:ok, count} = Updater.update()

    # Update from specific source
    {:ok, count} = Updater.update(source: "https://github.com/org/prompts")

    # Update with force overwrite

from pyannote.audio.pipelines.speaker_diarization import SpeakerDiarization
from pyannote.core import Segment
import sys, json

pipeline = SpeakerDiarization.from_pretrained("pyannote/speaker-diarization")

def process_audio(audio_file):
    diarization = pipeline(audio_file)
    results = [{"start": s.start, "end": s.end, "speaker": spk} for s, spk in diarization.itertracks()]
    print(json.dumps(results))

Utilities for UUID (Universally Unique Identifier) generation and manipulation.

This module provides basic functions to generate random UUIDs,
particularly in v4 (random) format.

UUIDs are useful for unique entity IDs, tracking operations across systems,
and ensuring identifier uniqueness without central coordination.

All functions are pure and concurrency-safe.

This module generates UUIDs based on strong cryptographic random bytes,
but does **not** strictly enforce RFC 4122 formatting (e.g., fixed version bits).
For strict compliance, external libraries like `:uuid` can be used.

    36

    ...> id2 = Prismatic.Utils.url_friendly_nanoid("test@example.com")

    ...> String.length(id) == 33
    true

Renders a tabbed navigation component.

## Slots

- `:tab`: A slot representing individual tabs. Each tab has the following attributes:
  - `:active` (boolean): Indicates if the tab is active.
  - `:patch` (any): The navigation target for the tab.

## Examples

    assigns = %{
      tab: [
        %{active: true, patch: "/", label: "Home", inner_block: nil},
        %{active: false, patch: "/about", label: "About", inner_block: nil}
      ],
      class: "custom-class"

    # This function does not directly return renderable HTML outside Phoenix templates.

The `PrismaticWeb.FallbackController` translates action results into valid `Plug.Conn` responses.

This controller provides a mechanism to handle errors and translate them into appropriate HTTP responses. It is used in conjunction with `Phoenix.Controller.action_fallback/1`.

## Features

- Handles `{:error, :not_found}` responses by rendering a 404 page.
- Handles generic errors with `{:error, reason}`.
- Handles unexpected cases where `nil` is returned.
- Extensible to handle additional error cases.

    # In a controller:
    action_fallback PrismaticWeb.FallbackController

    def show(conn, %{"id" => id}) do
      case MyApp.get_resource(id) do
        nil -> {:error, :not_found}
        resource -> render(conn, "show.html", resource: resource)
      end
    end

module_attributes.name: doc
module_attributes.value:
Handles mounting and authenticating the current_user in LiveViews.

## `on_mount` arguments

  * `:mount_current_user` - Assigns current_user
    to socket assigns based on user_token, or nil if
    there's no user_token or no matching user.

  * `:ensure_authenticated` - Authenticates the user from the session,
    and assigns the current_user to socket assigns based
    on user_token.
    Redirects to login page if there's no logged user.

  * `:redirect_if_user_is_authenticated` - Authenticates the user from the session.
    Redirects to signed_in_path if there's a logged user.

## Examples

Use the `on_mount` lifecycle macro in LiveViews to mount or authenticate
the current_user:

    defmodule PrismaticWeb.PageLive do
      use PrismaticWeb, :live_view

      on_mount {PrismaticWeb.UserAuth, :mount_current_user}
      ...
    end

Or use the `live_session` of your router to invoke the on_mount callback:

    live_session :authenticated, on_mount: [{PrismaticWeb.UserAuth, :ensure_authenticated}] do
      live "/profile", ProfileLive, :index
    end

Logs the user in.

It renews the session ID and clears the whole session
to avoid fixation attacks. See the renew_session
function to customize this behaviour.

It also sets a `:live_socket_id` key in the session,
so LiveView sessions are identified and automatically
disconnected on log out. The line can be safely removed
if you are not using LiveView.

Transcribes an audio file using the specified whisper model.

## Parameters
  * `model_path` - Path to the whisper model file (e.g., "models/ggml-base.en.bin")
  * `file_path` - Path to an audio file (should be 16kHz mono WAV)

  * `{:ok, text}` - On success, returns the transcribed text
  * `{:error, reason}` - On failure, returns an error with the reason

## Example

    PrismaticWhisper.transcribe_file("models/ggml-base.en.bin", "recording.wav")

## Parameters
  * `model_path` - Path to the whisper model file (e.g., "models/ggml-base.en.bin")
  * `audio_data` - List of float PCM audio samples (16kHz mono)

  * `{:ok, text}` - On success, returns the transcribed text

    PrismaticWhisper.transcribe_audio("models/ggml-base.en.bin", audio_data)

Starts a llama.cpp server with the specified model and configuration.

## Usage

    mix llama.server [options]

## Options

    --model         - Path to the model file to use (required if not in env)
    --dir           - Path to llama.cpp directory (default:

)
    --port          - Port to run the server on (default:

)
    --host          - Host to bind the server to (default:

)
    --gpu-layers    - Number of GPU layers to offload (default: 0)
    --threads       - Number of threads to use (default: auto)
    --chat-template - Chat template to use (default:

)
    --foreground    - Run in foreground instead of spawning a process
    --verbose       - Enable verbose output from the server

## Environment Variables

    LLAMA_MODEL_PATH - Default model path if --model is not specified
    LLAMA_PORT       - Default port if --port is not specified

## Examples

    # Start with default settings
    mix llama.server --model models/llama-3-8b.Q5_K_M.gguf

    # Start with custom settings
    mix llama.server --model models/llama-3-8b.Q5_K_M.gguf --port 8000 --context-size 4096 --gpu-layers 40

    # Start in foreground mode
    mix llama.server --model models/llama-3-8b.Q5_K_M.gguf --foreground
